days.title: Introducing Yourself Clearly
days.objective: Introduce yourself in a clear, well-paced 30-45 second self-introduction with no more than 2 filler words.

warmup.instructions: Take 4 slow breaths (inhale 4s, hold 2s, exhale 6s). Then loosen your jaw by opening your mouth wide 5 times and rolling your tongue around your lips 5 times each direction.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: She sells seashells by the seashore.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Say the drill sentence slowly 3 times, then at normal speed 3 times. Focus on crisp S and SH sounds without slurring.

mini_lesson.title: The 3-Part Self-Introduction
mini_lesson.content: A clear self-introduction has three parts: who you are, what you do, and one personal or interesting detail. Keeping it to three short sentences prevents rambling and filler words.
key_points: Part 1: Name and a brief identity ("I'm Sam, a marketing analyst.")
Part 2: What you do or are working on right now
Part 3: One personal detail that makes you memorable

vocabulary.meaning: able to express ideas clearly and effectively
vocabulary.example_sentence: She gave an articulate answer to a difficult question.

vocabulary.meaning: giving information in a few words; brief but complete
vocabulary.example_sentence: Try to keep your introduction concise, around 30 seconds.

vocabulary.meaning: a sound or word (um, uh, like) used to pause without meaning to add content
vocabulary.example_sentence: Try to notice every time you use a filler word today.

phrases: I currently work as ___ / I'm currently studying ___.
Something people don't usually know about me is ___.
I'm looking forward to improving my speaking over the next 30 days.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Record a 30-45 second self-introduction using the 3-part structure from today's mini lesson.
tips: Say your name clearly and pause briefly after it
Use at least one word from today's vocabulary list

conversation.opening_question: That was a great introduction! What made you decide to start this 30-day speaking practice?
follow_up_questions: What part of speaking clearly do you find hardest right now?
Is there a specific situation, like meetings or interviews, where you most want to sound clearer?
How would you describe your speaking confidence on a scale of 1 to 10 today?

feedback_criteria: clarity_score (pronunciation crispness on S/SH sounds from the drill)
structure_check (did the response include identity, activity, and a personal detail)
days.retry_instructions: If your filler-word count was above 2 or the response ran under 20 seconds, listen to your recording once, then retry focusing only on the 3-part structure — don't worry about sounding perfect.

days.title: Slowing Your Pace
days.objective: Deliver a 45-second answer at a steady 120-150 words per minute with at least three intentional pauses.

warmup.instructions: Box breathing: inhale 4s, hold 4s, exhale 4s, hold 4s. Repeat 4 rounds while keeping your shoulders relaxed.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Two tired toads tried to trot to town.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Read the drill at half speed, tapping the table on every T and D, then repeat at normal speed.

mini_lesson.title: The Power of the Pause
mini_lesson.content: Pauses are not empty space — they replace filler words and give the listener time to absorb your idea. A one-second pause feels long to you and natural to everyone else.
key_points: Pause after your main point, not in the middle of it

vocabulary.meaning: the rhythm and flow of the way you speak
vocabulary.example_sentence: His calm cadence made the presentation easy to follow.

vocabulary.meaning: done slowly and on purpose, with care
vocabulary.example_sentence: She spoke in a deliberate way so every word landed.

phrases: Let me take a moment on that.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Describe your morning routine for 45 seconds, pausing for a full second after each step.
tips: Count one full second in every pause

conversation.opening_question: Nice pacing. Where in your day do you tend to speak too fast?
follow_up_questions: What usually makes you rush — nerves, or a short meeting?
How did the one-second pause feel to you?

days.retry_instructions: If you rushed, retry with only three sentences and a long pause between each.

days.title: Cutting Filler Words
days.objective: Explain a familiar process for 60 seconds using no more than one filler word.

warmup.instructions: Hum a steady note for 10 seconds, five times, sliding gently from low to high pitch to open up resonance.

articulation_exercise.drill_text: Really rural lorry drivers rarely rally.
articulation_exercise.instructions: Repeat the drill 5 times, exaggerating the R and L tongue positions.

mini_lesson.title: Catch, Don't Punish
mini_lesson.content: Filler words disappear through awareness, not willpower. Noticing them as they happen retrains the habit faster than trying to force perfect speech.
key_points: Notice your personal filler (um, like, you know, basically)
Swap it for a closed mouth and a breath
Slower speech naturally produces fewer fillers

vocabulary.meaning: expressed clearly in very few words
vocabulary.example_sentence: Her succinct summary saved the meeting ten minutes.
The verbose answer buried the useful part.

phrases: The first step is ___, and then ___.
That's really all there is to it.

speaking_prompt.prompt: Explain how to make your favourite drink or dish, step by step, for 60 seconds.
tips: Stop and breathe instead of saying 'um'

conversation.opening_question: Clear steps! Which filler word do you catch yourself using most?
follow_up_questions: When does it show up most — under pressure or when you're unsure?
What would you like to say instead of it?

days.retry_instructions: Listen back and count your fillers, then retry the same explanation in three steps only.
